learn.b: In JavaScript a function is a value, so you can pass it to another function as an argument. A function you hand over to be called later is a callback. The function that receives it decides when to call it.

Many callbacks run immediately, in order, before the outer function finishes. Array methods like forEach, map and filter work this way. Passing different callbacks gives the same function different behaviour.

Some work takes time, like a timer or a network request. JavaScript does not wait: it keeps running the next lines and calls your callback when the work finishes. setTimeout(fn, ms) is the simplest example.

Node.js made a convention: the callback gets the error as its first argument, or null if all went well, and the result second. When callbacks nest inside callbacks the code drifts to the right and becomes hard to read. This pyramid is called callback hell, and promises were invented to fix it.

o: A function passed to another function to be called later

qs.why: It schedules fn to run after the delay.

learn.b: A promise is an object that stands for a result that is not ready yet. It starts pending and then settles: fulfilled with a value, or rejected with an error. Once settled it never changes.
Use .then(fn) to run code when the promise is fulfilled, .catch(fn) when it is rejected and .finally(fn) when it settles either way. Each of these returns a new promise, so you can chain them.
learn.code:
Promise.resolve(5)
  .then(n => n * 2)
  .then(n => console.log(n)) // 10
  .catch(e => console.log("error"))
  .finally(() => console.log("end"));

learn.b: Promise.all waits for every promise and gives an array of results, but rejects as soon as one fails. Promise.allSettled waits for all and reports each outcome as an object with a status. Promise.race settles with whichever promise finishes first.
learn.code:
Promise.all([Promise.resolve(1), Promise.resolve(2)])
  .then(r => console.log(r.join())); // 1,2

learn.b: Promise callbacks go into the microtask queue, which runs after the current code finishes but before timers. So synchronous code runs first, then promise callbacks, then setTimeout callbacks, even with a delay of 0.

qs.why: The three states are pending, fulfilled and rejected.

qs.q: What does .catch handle?
qs.why: .catch runs when the promise is rejected.

learn.b: Putting async before a function makes it always return a promise. Whatever you return becomes the value of that promise, and a thrown error becomes a rejection.

Inside an async function, await pauses that function until a promise settles and gives you its value. It reads like normal step-by-step code. Only that function waits: the rest of the program keeps running. await can only be used inside async functions (or at the top level of a module).

A rejected promise makes await throw, so you handle failures with normal try/catch. This is much cleaner than a long chain of .catch calls. A forgotten await is a common bug: you get a pending promise instead of the value.

Two awaits in a row run one after the other. If the tasks do not depend on each other, start them together and await Promise.all, which is faster. For loops of async work use for...of with await inside, or Promise.all with map to run them at once.

qs.q: What does an async function always return?
qs.why: The return value is wrapped in a promise.

qs.q: Where can await be used?
qs.why: await needs an async function (or a module top level).

learn.b: A Map stores key-value pairs like an object, but any value can be a key, it remembers insertion order and it has a size property. Use set(key, value), get(key), has(key) and delete(key). Getting a missing key gives undefined.
A Map is iterable. for...of gives [key, value] pairs, which you can destructure. m.keys() and m.values() give just the keys or values, and in the order they were added.
A Set holds unique values, so adding the same value twice does nothing. Use add, has, delete and size. Sets are perfect for removing duplicates and for fast is-it-in-here checks.
Spread a Set to turn it back into an array, which removes duplicates in one line. A Map is the natural tool for counting how often things appear: get the old count, add one and set it again.

qs.why: A Set never keeps duplicates.

learn.b: Something is iterable if for...of and the spread syntax can loop over it. Arrays, strings, Maps and Sets are iterable. Plain objects are not. Behind the scenes an iterable can produce an iterator.
learn.code:
for (const ch of "hi") console.log(ch);
console.log([..."abc"].length); // 3

learn.b: An iterator is an object with a next() method. Each call returns an object { value, done }. While there are items, done is false, and at the end done becomes true. for...of simply calls next() again and again.
learn.code:
const it = ["x", "y"][Symbol.iterator]();
console.log(it.next().value); // x
console.log(it.next().value); // y
console.log(it.next().done); // true

learn.b: A generator function is written function* and uses yield to hand out values one at a time. Calling it does not run the body yet. Each next() runs until the next yield and pauses there, remembering everything. Generators are iterable, so you can spread them.
Because a generator only works when asked, it can describe an infinite sequence without using infinite memory. You just take the values you need. This is called lazy evaluation.

qs.why: It returns { value, done }.

learn.b: When a browser loads a web page it builds the DOM, the Document Object Model. It is a tree of objects: the document at the top, then the html element, then the head and body and everything inside. JavaScript can read and change this tree, and the page updates on screen. The DOM belongs to the browser, not to the JavaScript language itself.
learn.code:
// document is the root object
console.log(typeof document); // in a browser: object

learn.b: document.querySelector takes a CSS selector and returns the first matching element, or null. querySelectorAll returns all of them. A selector like #title means the element with id title, .item means class item and p means every paragraph.

Set textContent to change the plain text of an element. Use classList.add, remove and toggle to change CSS classes, which is the best way to restyle. You can also set attributes and style properties directly. Avoid innerHTML with user text, because it can run harmful code.

createElement makes a new element that is not on the page yet. Fill it in and then add it with appendChild or append on a parent. remove() takes an element away again. This is how lists on a page are built from data.

qs.q: What does DOM stand for?
qs.why: It is the Document Object Model.

learn.b: An event is something that happens on the page: a click, a key press, typing in a box, a form being sent. You attach a function to an element with addEventListener(type, handler). The handler runs every time the event happens.

The browser passes an event object to your handler. event.target is the element that was clicked, event.key tells which key was pressed and for text boxes, event.target.value holds the current text. event.preventDefault() stops the browser default action, like a form reloading the page.

Most events bubble: after running on the target element they travel up through its parents. Because of this you can put one listener on a parent list and check event.target to see which child was clicked. This is event delegation, and it also works for elements added later.

learn.h: Removing and the idea behind it
learn.b: removeEventListener removes a handler, but you must pass the same function. Events work on the publish and subscribe idea: code registers interest with on and something announces it with emit. You can build this yourself with plain objects, with no browser needed.

learn.b: The web works by requests and responses. Your code sends a request to a URL, a server does some work and sends back a response. An API is a set of URLs a server offers so programs can ask for data, usually as JSON. The common methods are GET to read data and POST to send data.

Every response has a status code. 2xx means success (200 is OK), 3xx means redirect, 4xx means the request was wrong (404 Not Found, 401 not logged in, 403 not allowed) and 5xx means the server failed (500). fetch does not throw on 404 or 500, so you must check response.ok yourself.

fetch(url) returns a promise of a Response. Call response.json() to read the body, which is also a promise. Use async/await and try/catch so network errors are handled. For POST pass an options object with method, headers and a JSON body.

Extra data is added to a URL after a question mark, like ?q=cat&page=2, and special characters must be encoded with encodeURIComponent. Many APIs need an API key, which you must keep secret. Browsers also enforce CORS: a server must allow your page to read its responses, otherwise the browser blocks them.

qs.why: fetch returns a promise that resolves to a Response object.

learn.b: Node.js lets you run JavaScript on your computer or a server, without a browser. You run a file with node app.js in a terminal. There is no document or window, but you get tools for files, networks and the operating system. Typing just node opens a REPL where you try code line by line.

Node supports two module styles. CommonJS uses require and module.exports and is the older one. ES modules use import and export, the same as in the browser, when the file ends in .mjs or package.json says type is module. Built-in modules such as fs (files) and path are always available.
learn.code:
const fs = require("fs");        // CommonJS
// import fs from "fs";          // ES module

learn.b: npm is the package manager that comes with Node. npm init creates package.json, a file describing your project and its dependencies. npm install name downloads a package into node_modules and records it in package.json. Dependencies are needed to run the app and devDependencies only while developing.
learn.code:
npm init -y
npm install lodash
npm install --save-dev jest

learn.b: The scripts section of package.json holds shortcuts, so npm start runs the start script and npm run build runs build. Versions follow semver: major.minor.patch, like 1.4.2. Never commit node_modules to git. Your program can read command-line arguments from process.argv, and npx runs a package without installing it permanently.
learn.code:
{ "scripts": { "start": "node app.js" } }
// npm start  -> runs node app.js

qs.why: npm start runs the start script.

learn.b: Before writing functions, decide how the data looks. A todo list is an array of objects, each with an id, a text and a done flag. A score tracker is a Map or object from player name to total points. Good data makes the code simple.

learn.h: Small functions that return new data
learn.b: Write one small function per action: add, toggle, remove. Prefer functions that return a new array instead of changing the old one, using map and filter. That makes bugs easier to find and works well with UI libraries.

Do not store what you can calculate. The number of items left is just todos.filter(t => !t.done).length. A leaderboard is the entries sorted by score. Calculating on demand keeps the data from getting out of sync.
learn.code:
const left = todos.filter(t => !t.done).length;
const board = [...scores].sort((a, b) => b[1] - a[1]);

learn.b: Keep the logic in functions or a class that knows nothing about the page. Then the buttons and lists only call these functions and show the results. You can test the logic with console.log alone, which is what the challenges here do.
